units.text: MORPHISMS REPRESENTED BY MONOMORPHISMS WITH n-TORSIONFREE COKERNEL
Introduction

Throughout this paper, let R be a two-sided noetherian ring.We assume that all modules are finitely generated right ones.Denote by mod R the category of (finitely generated right) R-modules.It is a natural and classical question to ask when a given homomorphism of R-modules is stably equivalent to another homomorphism satisfying certain good properties.A well-studied one is about stable equivalence to a monomorphism: A homomorphism f : X → Y of R-modules is said to be represented by monomorphisms if there is an Rhomomorphism t : X → P with P projective such that f t : X → Y ⊕ P is a monomorphism.This notion has been introduced by Auslander and Bridger [1], and later studied in detail by Kato [9].Among other things, Kato gave the following characterization; we denote by Tr(−) the (Auslander) transpose.
Theorem 1.1 (Kato).Let f : X → Y be an R-homomorphism.Then the following are equivalent.
(1) The morphism f is represented by monomorphisms.

(2) The map Ext 1 R op (Tr f, R) : Ext 1 R op (Tr X, R) → Ext 1 R op (Tr Y, R) is injective.Motivated by the above theorem, we define a condition which we call (T n ) for each integer n 0 so that (T 1 ) is equivalent to being represented by monomorphisms, and find out several properties.The first main result is the following theorem, which recovers Theorem 1.1 as a special case.Theorem 1.2 (Theorems 3.6 and 3.9).Let n 1 be an integer.Consider the following conditions for an R-homomorphism f : X → Y .

(a n ) The homomorphism f satisfies (T n ).(a ′ n ) There is an R-homomorphism t : X → P with P projective such that the map f t : X → Y ⊕ P is a monomorphism whose cokernel is (n − 1)-torsionfree and whose R-dual is surjective.
n ) There is an R-homomorphism t : X → P with P projective such that the map f t : X → Y ⊕ P is a monomorphism whose cokernel is (n − 1)-torsionfree.(b n ) The kernel of the map (f, s) :
X ⊕ Q → Y is n-torsionfree for any epimorphism s : Q → Y with Q projective. (c n ) The kernel of the map Ext 1 R (f, R) : Ext 1 R (Y, R) → Ext 1 R (X, R
) has grade at least n.Then the following implications hold.
Moreover, the implications (a n ) ⇔ (a ′ n ) ⇒ (a ′′ n ) hold, and the implication (a ′′ n ) ⇒ (a n ) is also true if the (n − 1)-torsionfree property is closed under extensions.

The notion of n-torsionfree modules was also introduced by Auslander and Bridger [1], and played a central role in the theory they developed.For example, for an R-module M , Auslander and Bridger figured out the relationship between the grade of the Ext module Ext i R (M, R) and the torsionfreeness of the syzygy Ω i M .
This result has been playing an important role in studies on n-torsionfree modules.(1) The inequality grade R op Ext i R (M, R) i + j − 1 holds for all 1 i n.
(2) The syzygy Ω i M is i-torsionfree and the natural map ψ i M : Tr Ω i Tr Ω i M → M satisfies (T j ) for all 1 i n.

Finally, let us consider the case where R is commutative.The local Gorensteinness of commutative rings is an actively studied subject in commutative algebra.For example, the relationship between the local Gorensteinness of the ring R and the structure of the category of n-torsionfree modules has been well-studied; see [1,5,6,7,10] for instance.Using the above theorem, we can also interpret the (local) Gorensteinness in terms of the natural maps ψ i M : Tr Ω i Tr Ω i M → M being represented by monomorphisms as follows.Corollary 1.4 (Proposition 5.2 and Corollary 5.3).Suppose that R is commutative.
(1) Assume that R is local and with depth t.Let k be the residue field of R. The following are equivalent.
(i) The ring R is Gorenstein.
(ii) The natural map ψ t+1 M : Tr Ω t+1 Tr Ω t+1 M → M is represented by monomorphisms for all R-modules M . (iii) The natural map ψ t+1 k : Tr Ω t+1 Tr Ω t+1 k → k is represented by monomorphisms.
(2) Let n 1 be an integer.The following are equivalent.

(i) The localization R p is Gorenstein for all prime ideals p with depth R p < n (ii) The natural map ψ i M : Tr Ω i Tr Ω i M → M is represented by monomorphisms for all R-modules M and for all integers 1 i n.

The organization of this paper is as follows.In Section 2, we state several notions and their basic properties for later use.In Section 3, we give the definition of the condition (T n ).We derive its basic properties and prove Theorem 1.2.In Section 4, we recall the construction of the natural map ψ i M : Tr Ω i Tr Ω i M → M , and apply a result obtained in Section 3 to ψ i M .We show Theorem 1.3 in this section.In the final Section 5, we describe local Gorensteinness of commutative rings in terms of ψ i M being represented by monomorphisms.
Preliminaries

The notion of n-torsionfree modules was introduced by Auslander and Bridger [1], and played a central role in the stable module theory they developed.It is also an important concept in this paper.Definition 2.5.(1) Let n 0 be an integer.An R-module X is said to be n-torsionfree if Ext i R op (Tr X, R) = 0 for all 1 i n.We denote by TF n (R) the full subcategory of mod R consisting of n-torsionfree modules.

We recall the definitions of heights and depths.The details can be found in [11].
Definition 2.6.Suppose that R is commutative.

(1) The height of a prime ideal p of R, denoted by ht p, is defined to be the supremum of the lengths of all strictly decreasing chains of prime ideals contained in p. (2) When R is a local ring with maximal ideal m, the depth of an R-module M is defined to be the infimum of integers i such that Ext i R (R/m, M ) = 0, and denoted by depth R M .We recall the definitions of Serre's condition (S n ) and the local Gorensteinness condition (G n ).These conditions are related to the n-torsionfreeness of modules; see [1,6,7,10] for instance.Definition 2.7.Suppose that R is commutative.Let n be an integer.
(1) Let M be an R-module.We say that M satisfies Serre's condition (S n ) if the inequality depth Rp M p min{n, ht p} holds for all prime ideals p of R.
(2) We say that R satisfies (G n ) if the localization R p is a Gorenstein local ring for all prime ideals p of R with ht p n.
Remark 2.8.Let n 0 be an integer.
(1) Let M be an R-module.We denote by ϕ M : M → M * * the canonical map given by ϕ

M (x)(f ) = f (x) for x ∈ M and f ∈ M * . By [1, Proposition 2.6], M is 1-torsionfree if and only if ϕ M is injective, that is, M is torsionless. Similarly, M is 2-torsionfree if and only if ϕ M is bijective, that is, M is reflexive. (2)
All n-torsionfree modules are n-syzygy; see [1, Theorem 2.17].
(3) Suppose that R is commutative.If R satisfies (S n ), then so do all the n-syzygy modules.This assertion is proved by the depth lemma [4, Proposition 1.2.9].
The condition (T n )

We begin with introducing the new condition (T n ) for R-homomorphisms.It is a natural extension of the condition (2) in Theorem 1.1.Definition 3.1.Let n 1 be an integer.We say that a homomorphism f :
X → Y of R-modules satisfies (T n ) if the map Ext i R op (Tr f, R) is bijective for all 1 i n − 1 and Ext n R op (Tr f, R) is injective.
In addition, we provide that every R-homomorphism satisfies (T 0 ) and an R-homomorphism f satisfies (T ∞ ) if f satisfies (T n ) for all n 0.
In this section, we explore those homomorphisms which satisfy the condition (T n ).Below we give several statements which easily follow by definition.
Remark 3.2. Let f : X → Y , f ′ : X ′ → Y ′ and g : Y → Z be R-homomorphisms.
Let n 1 be an integer.
(1) Suppose that f ≈ f ′ .Then f satisfies (T n ) if and only if so does f ′ .
(2) If g and f satisfy (T n ), then gf satisfies (T n ).
(3) If gf satisfies (T 1 ), then f satisfies (T 1 ).In general, if gf and g satisfy (T n ), then f satisfies (T n ).( 4) Consider the following conditions.
(a n ) The homomorphism f satisfies (T n ). (b n ) The module X is n-torsionfree. (c n ) The module Y is n-torsionfree.
Then the following implications hold.
(5) Stable isomorphisms satisfy (T ∞ ).

Now, let us investigate the condition (T 1 ).Kato [9, Theorem 3.9] proved the following theorem, which asserts that (T 1 ) is equivalent to being represented by monomorphisms, using the homotopy theory developed in [9, Sections 2 and 3].Using [1, Proposition 2.6], we can provide another simpler proof of Kato's theorem as follows.
Theorem 3.3 (Kato).Let f : X → Y be a homomorphism of R-modules.The following are equivalent.
(1) The homomorphism f is represented by monomorphisms, i.e., there is an R-homomorphism t : X → P with P projective such that f t :

X → Y ⊕ P is a monomorphism. (2) The homomorphism f satisfies (T 1 ). (3) One has Ker f ∩ Ker ϕ X = 0. Proof. We have a commutative diagram 0 0 0 / / Ker f ∩ Ker ϕ X / / Ker f 0 / / Ker ϕ X / / f X ϕX / / f X * * 0 / / Ker ϕ Y / / Y ϕY / / Y * *

Therefore, one has Ker f ∩ Ker ϕ X ∼ = Ker Ext 1 (Tr f, R) and we have the equivalence (2) ⇔ (3).

Next, suppose that (1) holds, i.e., there is a homomorphism t : X → P with P projective such that f t is injective.As Ker f t ∩ Ker ϕ X = 0, we obtain that f t satisfies (T 1 ).Thus f also satisfies (T 1 ), and the implication (1) ⇒ (2) follows.

Finally, assume that (3) holds and take a left proj R-approximation t : X → P of X.Then we see that Ker ϕ X = Ker t.We have Ker f t = Ker f ∩ Ker t = Ker f ∩ Ker ϕ X = 0, that is, f t is injective.Therefore, the implication (3) ⇒ (1) holds and we are done.
